items.title: The Smartest People of Classical Antiquity
items.description:
Who were the smartest people in the ancient world?
Classical antiquity was a period spanning over several centuries and encompassing various cultures and civilizations, so it is difficult to identify a single person as the "smartest." Moreover, intelligence can manifest itself in various forms and domains, such as philosophy, science, mathematics, literature, and politics, among others.

There were several notable figures in classical antiquity who made significant contributions to various field
items.why_watch: This is a compact survey of intellectual giants across classical antiquity — philosophers, mathematicians, engineers — with the honest acknowledgment that 'smartest' means different things across domains and cultures. It won't replace a deep-dive into any single figure, but it works well as a map for deciding whose work you actually want to explore further. A solid 23 minutes if you're filling gaps in your ancient history mental model.

items.why_watch: The central argument here is genuinely surprising: individual biological neurons, thanks to the branching complexity of their dendrites, may themselves perform computations equivalent to a multi-layer neural network — meaning your brain could be far more powerful than standard neuroscience models suggest. Harvard PhD student Artem Kirsanov explains the underlying research clearly, with strong animations, without dumbing it down. This reframes how you think about the relationship between biological and artificial intelligence.

items.title: neanderthals were smarter than we think || a prehistoric family and how they went extinct
items.description: i talk about a recent article published which gives us a look at a possible neanderthal family living all 2gether. also other stuff.
items.why_watch: This video covers a recent study that identified what may be an actual Neanderthal family group from fossil evidence — father, daughters, cousins — giving a startlingly intimate window into their social lives. The creator, fig tree, has a relaxed, conversational style that makes the science feel approachable without losing the substance, and she's careful to distinguish what the evidence actually shows from speculation. It quietly dismantles the 'brutish caveman' stereotype with specifics rather than generalities.

discovery_articles.title: Rogue Creamery  in Central Point, Oregon
discovery_articles.snippet: The Rogue Creamery in Central Point, Oregon is worth a detour for fabulous world-class cheeses. The building in itself is cute enough to stop for a photo op with a vintage mural, blue neon sign, and old blue pickup truck advertising this cheese monger paradise. But what lays inside is a humble but extraordinary cheese selection ranging from cheese curds, wheels of Rogue Blue cheese (this is the world winning), and you can even order a decadent grilled cheese to enjoy patio-side.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Rogue Creamery's world-champion blue cheese is made just a short drive from the California border in a town most people pass straight through — proof that extraordinary things hide in the unhurried places. The vintage pickup truck out front is charming, but it's the cave-aged wheels inside that are genuinely worth pulling over for.

news.title: Kinz, London W11: ‘No bells, no whistles, just Lebanese food cooked with immense pride’ – restaurant review
news.snippet: Home cooking, but in the most complimentary sense Some developers would rip the soul out of a 1930s banking hall, but Kinz , a new all-day Lebanese brasserie housed in a former Lloyds Bank in Notting Hill, instead makes a feature of its chunky vault door. Where W11 residents once kept their cash, diners can now take a seat and sip Lebanese wine from the Bekaa valley . After all, what visit to the bank wouldn’t be improved by a cold glass of Chateau Musar Jeune ?
news.blurb: Lebanese food cooked with quiet conviction in a former bank — The Guardian's review of Kinz is a reminder that the best restaurants have nothing to prove and everything to offer.
